title: Fine bodies, empty words
hook: their bodies impress you and their speech charms you, but they're like propped-up timber (63:4)

segments.voice: Yesterday, then go out and seek, and your line was pray, then work. Did your next task get done a little better? Today, Surah Al-Munafiqun. Day six hundred twenty-eight.

Walk through a film set and you'll see a whole street: shop fronts, balconies, a church tower. Walk around the back and it's plywood and scaffolding, held up by diagonal beams. From the front, perfect. From behind, nothing. Surah sixty-three is about people in Medina who were a little like that street. It's named for them: Al-Munafiqun. And in one verse, it gives them an image so vivid it's hard to forget.

Verse four. Pickthall: "And when thou seest them their figures please thee; and if they speak thou givest ear unto their speech. (They are) as though they were blocks of wood in striped cloaks." The Arabic image is khushubun musannadah: timber propped up against a wall. Wood that looks solid, but can't stand on its own, with nothing living in it. Fine bodies, polished words, and inside, no root. The word for what the surah describes is nifaq. Classical Arabic dictionaries connect it to the nafiqa', a burrow some desert animals dig with a hidden second exit: one way in that everyone sees, and another way out that no one does. Nifaq is having two doors. In the Qur'an, the munafiqun are people who declared faith in Medina while working against the community in secret. But the hadith also turns the word into a mirror for believers. Bukhari records the Prophet ﷺ naming the signs: when he speaks, he lies; when he promises, he breaks it; when he's trusted, he betrays. And Muslim records a tender scene. A companion named Hanzala ran to Abu Bakr crying, Hanzala has become a hypocrite! With the Prophet, he said, he felt paradise and hell before his eyes; at home with his wife and children, he forgot. Abu Bakr said, I feel the same. They went to the Prophet, who told them: if you stayed always as you are with me, angels would shake your hands in the street. But Hanzala, an hour and an hour. The fear of being two-faced isn't nifaq. It's the conscience doing its work.
screen: `PROPPED-UP TIMBER.` · `NIFAQ: A BURROW WITH TWO DOORS.` · `LIES, BROKEN PROMISES, BETRAYAL.` · `HANZALA: AN HOUR AND AN HOUR.`

segments.voice: The practice: check your words against your deeds. Sit, and breathe. Gently, without harshness, look at one place where your outside and inside don't match: something you say you value but rarely do, or a face you wear in one room and not another. Don't scold yourself. Hanzala's worry was a good sign. Just name it, and choose one small way to bring the two sides a little closer. The bell holds the time.
Nifaq. Hypocrisy: a burrow with two doors, a fine front with timber propped up behind it. Today's word.
Your line: not propped up. Today, do one thing that matches what you say you care about, where no one will see it. Day six hundred twenty-eight.

screen: `DAY 628 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: DON'T LET THEM DISTRACT YOU.`

howItsDone: Muslim teachers often use the signs of the hypocrite from the hadith as a checklist for self-examination, and the story of Hanzala is told to reassure believers that changing moods are not hypocrisy.

original.note: Arabic: nifaq, hypocrisy. munafiqun are those who practice it; dictionaries link the root to a burrow with two exits.

trapdoor: what you thought: hypocrisy means saying one thing and doing another.
what it means: a fine front with nothing alive behind it, like timber propped against a wall.
what a scholar hears: khushub musannada in 63:4; the lexical link to nafiqa' (Lisan al-'Arab); the signs in Bukhari 33; Hanzala's 'sa'atan wa sa'atan' in Muslim 2750.
